newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Back in Russia, Lebed renews criticism of NATO.
newsitem.headline: Back in Russia, Lebed renews criticism of NATO.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed on Thursday launched a new broadside against NATO's plans to expand eastwards, one day after winning praise from the Western alliance during a trip to its headquarters.
"Will NATO's eastward expansion, towards our borders, towards the Baltic republics boost Russia's security?" Itar-Tass quoted Lebed as telling a scientific conference.
"Nobody can guarantee that it won't occur to someone at some time to do to us what was recently done to Iraq."

Lebed, who is President Boris Yeltsin's national security adviser, appeared to be referring to U.S. missile attacks on Iraqi military targets last month after Baghdad sent troops into a quasi-autonomous Kurdish zone in Iraq.

NATO officials had praised Lebed's stance during talks in Brussels this week on the alliance's plans to expand to take in countries of eastern and central Europe. Russia says such moves would threaten its security and opposes expansion.
Lebed drove home Moscow's message during his visit to Brussels but did not resort to the strong language which he had used in outbursts against NATO enlargement before the trip.

Lebed, who is jostling for position while Yeltsin is out of the Kremlin awaiting heart surgery, has been accused in Moscow of achieving little in his trip and had been widely expected to take a tougher public stance over NATO once he came home.
The gruff reserve general also had tough words over what he described as an arms build-up in Asia, but Tass did not single out any country for attack in its report of the speech.
"No one in the world plans to disarm except Russia. On the contrary, the arms race is being ascribed to more firmly in east, central and south Asia," Lebed was quoted as saying.

In a new appeal for more government funds to help Russia's depleted armed forces, he said there was enough money to go round for both the army and industry. Tass did not say if he had offered any details of where the money would come from.
Lebed, who has been in the Krmelin less than four months, also hit out against a lack of vision over Russia's security needs and interests.
"We have no concept of state security," he said.
